title: Rantideva's last cup of water
hookLine: after a long fast, a king finally sits down to a meal, and the guests start arriving
carry: the guest is God, down to the last one

lines: A LONG FAST, THEN A MEAL.
cards: A king who has already given away everything he owns sits down to eat. He and his family have gone a long stretch without food, without even water.
Now, at last, a meal: a little ghee, some milk, a porridge, a cup of water. Hands reach for the bowls. And then someone comes to the door.
The king is Rantideva, and the Bhagavata's ninth book tells his story in a handful of verses. It's a short story. It doesn't feel short when you're the one holding the bowl.

teach.b: The first to come is a brahmin guest. Rantideva sees God in his guest and feeds him gladly. That's the old Hindu rule families still repeat, atithi devo bhava: the guest is God.
He divides what's left with his family, and another guest arrives, a laborer, and he feeds him too.
Then comes a man with a pack of hungry dogs, and Rantideva gives him the rest of the food, honoring the man and the dogs alike.

teach.h: ONLY WATER LEFT, AND HE GIVES IT.
teach.b: Now only water is left. One more person comes, a man his society shut out as an outcaste, dying of thirst, asking for water. Rantideva, nearly dying of thirst himself, gives it.
Then he says the words the story is remembered for. In paraphrase: I don't ask God for the highest state, with all its powers, nor even for freedom from rebirth.

teach.h: NOT HEAVEN, NOT FREEDOM: THEIR PAIN.
teach.b: I ask to stand inside all beings and bear their pain, so that they can be free of it. Then a turn.
The guests, the story says, were the lords of the worlds themselves, come in disguise. They reveal themselves, ready to grant anything. Rantideva bows, and asks for nothing.

Two things for a vocation of seva. Every guest gets the same honor: the line runs from the honored to the shunned, and his care doesn't shrink as he goes down it. And he doesn't serve to get somewhere.
Not heaven, not even freedom. The service is the destination.

how: Rantideva's story from the Bhagavata's ninth book is told by Hindu teachers as a picture of selfless service, and his wish to bear the pain of all beings is quoted in talks on compassion and seva.

o: service for life, giving each guest equal honor
a reward the gods give to generous kings
a fast kept to earn freedom from rebirth

p: a king who gave everything away
given the rest of the food
asks for water, and gets it
to bear the pain of all beings

s: Rantideva asks God for freedom from rebirth as his reward
he says he wants neither the highest state nor freedom from rebirth, only to bear the pain of all beings.
Rantideva gives away even his last water
to a thirsty man his society shut out, while he himself was dying of thirst.
in the story, the guests turn out to be gods
they reveal themselves and offer anything; he asks for nothing.

games.q: you're Rantideva. after a long fast, only water is left, and you're dying of thirst. a man at the door begs for water. what do you do?
o: give him half and keep half.
games.why: he gives it all, and says he asks not for heaven or freedom but to bear the pain of all beings so they can be free of it.

practice: Picture a small meal on a table, yours, and let people you know come to the door one at a time: someone easy to give to, someone harder, someone you'd usually walk past.
You don't have to hand anything over; just notice the moment of reluctance with each one, and breathe through it. If you pray, you can hold each guest before the One you pray to.

wordCard.voice: Seva as vocation. Service as a whole life: Rantideva gives each guest the same honor, down to the last cup of water, and asks nothing back.

orig.note: Sanskrit: the name of the king in the Bhagavata's ninth book who gave his last food and water to his guests.

carryVoice: Your line: the guest is God, down to the last one. Honor doesn't run out before the last guest. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Bhagavata Purana 9.21.2–10 (Rantideva's fast; the meal; the brahmin, the shudra, the man with dogs, the pulkasa asking for water)
Bhagavata Purana 9.21.12–13 (I do not desire the highest goal with its powers, nor freedom from rebirth; I take on the suffering of all beings so they may be free of it)
Bhagavata Purana 9.21.15–17 (the guests were the lords of the worlds; Rantideva asks for nothing)
Taittiriya Upanishad 1.11.2 (atithi devo bhava: let the guest be as God to you; cited for the familiar phrase only)
